questions.problem: Given that $x=5$ is a solution to the equation ${x}^{3}-9{x}^{2}+29x-45=0,$ find the remaining solutions.
questions.worked_solution:
Let $f(x)={x}^{3}-9{x}^{2}+29x-45.$ Since $x=5$ is a root of $f(x),$ then according to the factor theorem $(x-5)$ is a factor of $f(x).$ 

We find the quotient when $f(x)$ is divided by $(x-5)$ using synthetic division.

$$
\begin{aligned}\enclose{bottom right}{5} & 1 & -9 & 29 & -45 \\  &  & 5 & -20 & 45 \\  & 1 & -4 & 9 & 0\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, $f(x)=(x-5)({x}^{2}-4x+9).$ 

To find the remaining two roots, we solve ${x}^{2}-4x+9=0$ by completing the square:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}-4x+9 & =0 \\ {x}^{2}-4x+4+5 & =0 \\ (x-2)^{2}+5 & =0 \\ (x-2)^{2} & =-5 \\ (x-2)^{2} & =(\sqrt{5}\text{i})^{2} \\ x-2 & =\pm \sqrt{5}\text{i} \\ x & =2\pm \sqrt{5}\text{i}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solutions to our original equation are $x=5,\,2\pm \sqrt{5}\text{i}.$

questions.problem: Given that $x=-\frac{1}{4}$ is a solution to the equation $36{x}^{3}+9{x}^{2}+4x+1=0,$ find the remaining solutions.
questions.worked_solution:
Let $f(x)=36{x}^{3}+9{x}^{2}+4x+1.$ Since $x=-\frac{1}{4}$ is a root of $f(x),$ then according to the factor theorem $(x+\frac{1}{4})$ is a factor of $f(x).$ 

We find the quotient when $f(x)$ is divided by $(x+\frac{1}{4})$ using synthetic division.

|  | ${x}^{3}$ | ${x}^{2}$ | ${x}^{1}$ | ${x}^{0}$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $-\frac{1}{4}$ | $36$ | $9$ | $4$ | $1$ |
|  | $↓$ | $-9$ | $0$ | $-1$ |
|  | $36$ | $0$ | $4$ | $0$ |

Thus, $f(x)=(x+\frac{1}{4})(36{x}^{2}+4).$ 

To find the remaining two roots, we solve $36{x}^{2}+4=0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}36{x}^{2}+4 & =0 \\ 36{x}^{2} & =-4 \\ {x}^{2} & =-\frac{1}{9} \\ {x}^{2} & ={(\frac{1}{3}\text{i})}^{2} \\ x & =\pm \frac{1}{3}\text{i}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solutions to our original equation are $x=-\frac{1}{4},\,\pm \frac{1}{3}\text{i}.$

We find the quotient when $f(x)$ is divided by $(x+\frac{1}{4})$ using synthetic division.

|  | ${x}^{3}$ | ${x}^{2}$ | ${x}^{1}$ | ${x}^{0}$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $-\frac{1}{4}$ | $4$ | $1$ | $100$ | $25$ |
|  | $↓$ | $-1$ | $0$ | $-25$ |
|  | $4$ | $0$ | $100$ | $0$ |

Thus, $f(x)=(x+\frac{1}{4})(4{x}^{2}+100).$

Therefore, the solutions to our original equation are $x=-\frac{1}{4},\,\pm 5\text{i}.$

questions.problem: Given that $x=-10$ is a solution to the equation ${x}^{3}+6{x}^{2}-24x+160=0,$ find the remaining solutions.
questions.worked_solution:
Let $f(x)={x}^{3}+6{x}^{2}-24x+160.$ Since $x=-10$ is a root of $f(x),$ then according to the factor theorem $(x+10)$ is a factor of $f(x).$ 

We find the quotient when $f(x)$ is divided by $(x+10)$ using synthetic division.

$$
\begin{aligned}\enclose{bottom right}{-10} & 1 & 6 & -24 & 160 \\  &  & -10 & 40 & -160 \\  & 1 & -4 & 16 & 0\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, $f(x)=(x+10)({x}^{2}-4x+16).$ 

To find the remaining two roots, we solve ${x}^{2}-4x+16=0$ by completing the square:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}-4x+16 & =0 \\ {x}^{2}-4x+4+12 & =0 \\ (x-2)^{2}+12 & =0 \\ (x-2)^{2} & =-12 \\ (x-2)^{2} & =(2\sqrt{3}\text{i})^{2} \\ x-2 & =\pm 2\sqrt{3}\text{i} \\ x & =2\pm 2\sqrt{3}\text{i}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solutions to our original equation are $x=-10,\,2\pm 2\sqrt{3}\text{i}.$

questions.problem: Given that $x=\frac{1}{3}$ is a solution to the equation $3{x}^{3}-7{x}^{2}+8x-2=0,$ find the remaining solutions.
questions.worked_solution:
Let $f(x)=9{x}^{3}-21{x}^{2}+24x-6.$ Since $x=\frac{1}{3}$ is a root of $f(x),$ then according to the factor theorem $(x-\frac{1}{3})$ is a factor of $f(x).$ 

We find the quotient when $f(x)$ is divided by $(x-\frac{1}{3})$ using synthetic division.

$$
\begin{aligned}\enclose{bottom right}{\frac{1}{3}} & 3 & -7 & 8 & -2 \\  &  & 1 & -2 & 2 \\  & 3 & -6 & 6 & 0\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, $f(x)=(x-\frac{1}{3})(3{x}^{2}-6x+6).$ 

To find the remaining two roots, we solve $3{x}^{2}-6x+6=0$ by completing the square:

$$
\begin{aligned}3{x}^{2}-6x+6 & =0 \\ 3({x}^{2}-2x+2) & =0 \\ {x}^{2}-2x+2 & =0 \\ {x}^{2}-2x+1+1 & =0 \\ (x-1)^{2}+1 & =0 \\ (x-1)^{2} & =-1 \\ (x-1)^{2} & =(\text{i})^{2} \\ x-1 & =\pm \text{i} \\ x & =1\pm \text{i}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solutions to our original equation are $x=\frac{1}{3},\,1\pm \text{i}.$

questions.problem: Find all of the solutions to $2{x}^{3}-9{x}^{2}+20x-8=0$ given that $x=2-2\text{i}$ is a solution.
questions.worked_solution:
First, we let $f(x)=2{x}^{3}-9{x}^{2}+20x-8.$ 

Since $f(x)$ has real coefficients and ${x}_{1}=2-2\text{i}$ is a root of $f(x),$ the complex conjugate 

$$
\overset{―}{{x}_{1}}=\overset{―}{2-2\text{i}}=2+2\text{i}
$$

must also be a root of $f(x).$

Now, according to the factor theorem, 
$(x-(2-2\text{i}))(x-(2+2\text{i}))$
is a factor of $f(x).$ Expanding the parentheses, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}(x-(2-2\text{i}))(x-(2+2\text{i})) & = \\ {x}^{2}-(2-2\text{i}+2+2\text{i})x+(2-2\text{i})(2+2\text{i}) & = \\ {x}^{2}-4x+({2}^{2}-(2\text{i})^{2}) & = \\ {x}^{2}-4x+8 & .\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we find the quotient when $f(x)$ is divided by ${x}^{2}-4x+8$ using polynomial division.

$$
\begin{aligned} & \,\,\,\,\,\,2x-1 \\  & {x}^{2}-4x+8\,\,\enclose{longdiv}{\,\,2{x}^{3}-9{x}^{2}+20x-8\,\,} \\  & \,\,\,\,\,\,{2{x}^{3}-8{x}^{2}+16x}_{―} \\  & \,\,\,\,\,\,-{x}^{2}+4x-8 \\  & \,\,\,\,\,\,\,{-\,{x}^{2}+4x-8}_{―} \\  & \,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,0\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, $f(x)=({x}^{2}-4x+8)(2x-1).$ 

To find the remaining root, we set the linear factor equal to zero and solve for $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}2x-1=0\,⟹\,x=\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the roots are $x=\frac{1}{2},2\pm 2\text{i}.$

questions.problem: Find all of the solutions to ${x}^{3}-4{x}^{2}-2x+20=0$ given that $x=3-\text{i}$ is a solution.
questions.worked_solution:
First, we let $f(x)={x}^{3}-4{x}^{2}-2x+20.$ 

Since $f(x)$ has real coefficients and ${x}_{1}=3-\text{i}$ is a root of $f(x),$ the complex conjugate 

$$
\overset{―}{{x}_{1}}=\overset{―}{3-\text{i}}=3+\text{i}
$$

must also be a root of $f(x).$

Now, according to the factor theorem, 
$(x-(3-\text{i}))(x-(3+\text{i}))$
is a factor of $f(x).$ Expanding the parentheses, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}(x-(3-\text{i}))(x-(3+\text{i})) & = \\ {x}^{2}-(3-\text{i}+(3+\text{i)})x+(3-\text{i})(3+\text{i}) & = \\ {x}^{2}-6x+({3}^{2}-(\text{i})^{2}) & = \\ {x}^{2}-6x+10 & .\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we find the quotient when $f(x)$ is divided by ${x}^{2}-6x+10$ using polynomial division.

$$
\begin{aligned} & \,\,\,\,\,x+2 \\  & {x}^{2}-6x+10\,\,\enclose{longdiv}{\,{x}^{3}-4{x}^{2}-2x+20} \\  & \,\,\,\,\,{{x}^{3}-6{x}^{2}+10x}_{―} \\  & \,\,\,\,\,2{x}^{2}-12x+20 \\  & \,\,\,\,\,{2{x}^{2}-12x+20}_{―} \\  & \,\,\,\,\,\,\,0\end{aligned}
$$

     

Thus, $f(x)=({x}^{2}-6x+10)(x+2).$ 

To find the remaining root, we set the linear factor equal to zero and solve for $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}x+2=0\,⟹\,x=-2.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the roots are $x=-2,3\pm \text{i}.$

questions.problem: Find all of the solutions to ${x}^{3}-{x}^{2}+9x-9=0$ given that $x=-3\text{i}$ is a solution.
questions.worked_solution:
First, we let $f(x)={x}^{3}-{x}^{2}+9x-9.$ 

Since $f(x)$ has real coefficients and ${x}_{1}=-3\text{i}$ is a root of $f(x),$ the complex conjugate 

$$
\overset{―}{{x}_{1}}=\overset{―}{-3\text{i}}=3\text{i}
$$

must also be a root of $f(x).$

Now, according to the factor theorem, 
$(x-3\text{i})(x-(-3\text{i}))$
is a factor of $f(x).$ Expanding the parentheses, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}(x-3\text{i})(x-(-3\text{i})) & ={x}^{2}+(3\text{i})(-3\text{i}) \\  & ={x}^{2}+9.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we find the quotient when $f(x)$ is divided by ${x}^{2}+9$ using polynomial division.

$$
\begin{aligned} & \,\,\,\,\,\,x-1\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\, \\  & {x}^{2}+9\,\,\enclose{longdiv}{\,\,{x}^{3}-{x}^{2}+9x-9\,} \\  & \,\,\,\,\,\,{{x}^{3}+9x}_{―} \\  & -{x}^{2}\,\,-9 \\  & \,{-\,{x}^{2}\,\,-9}_{―} \\  & \,\,\,\,0\end{aligned}
$$

  

Thus, $f(x)=({x}^{2}+9)(x-1).$ 

To find the remaining root, we set the linear factor equal to zero and solve for $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}x-1=0\,⟹\,x=1.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the roots are $x=1,\pm 3\text{i}.$

questions.problem: Find all of the solutions to ${x}^{3}+6{x}^{2}-11x-116=0$ given that $x=-5+2\text{i}$ is a solution.
questions.worked_solution:
First, we let $f(x)={x}^{3}+6{x}^{2}-11x-116.$

Since $f(x)$ has real coefficients and ${x}_{1}=-5+2\text{i}$ is a root of $f(x),$ the complex conjugate 

$$
\overset{―}{{x}_{1}}=\overset{―}{-5+2\text{i}}=-5-2\text{i}
$$

must also be a root of $f(x).$

Now, according to the factor theorem, 
$(x-(-5+2\text{i}))(x-(-5-2\text{i}))$
is a factor of $f(x).$ Expanding the parentheses, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}(x-(-5+2\text{i}))(x-(-5-2\text{i})) & = \\ {x}^{2}-(-5+2\text{i}+(-5-2\text{i)})x+(-5+2\text{i})(-5-2\text{i}) & = \\ {x}^{2}+10x+((-5)^{2}-(2\text{i})^{2}) & = \\ {x}^{2}+10x+29 & .\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we find the quotient when $f(x)$ is divided by ${x}^{2}+10x+29$ using polynomial division.

$$
\begin{aligned} & \,\,\,\,\,x-4 \\  & {x}^{2}+10x+29\,\,\enclose{longdiv}{\,{x}^{3}+6{x}^{2}-11x-116} \\  & \,\,\,\,\,{{x}^{3}+10{x}^{2}+29x}_{―} \\  & \,\,\,\,-4{x}^{2}+40x-116 \\  & \,\,\,{-4{x}^{2}+40x-116}_{―} \\  & \,\,\,\,0\end{aligned}
$$

        

Thus, $f(x)=({x}^{2}+10x+29)(x-4).$ 

To find the remaining root, we set the linear factor equal to zero and solve for $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}x-4=0\,⟹\,x=4.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the roots are $x=4,-5\pm 2\text{i}.$

questions.worked_solution:
First, we let $f(x)={x}^{3}-{x}^{2}+25x-25.$ 

Since $f(x)$ has real coefficients and ${x}_{1}=5\text{i}$ is a root of $f(x),$ the complex conjugate 

$$
\overset{―}{{x}_{1}}=\overset{―}{5\text{i}}=-5\text{i}
$$

must also be a root of $f(x).$

Now, according to the factor theorem, $(x-5\text{i})(x-(-5\text{i}))$ is a factor of $f(x).$ Expanding the parentheses, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}(x-5\text{i})(x-(-5\text{i})) & ={x}^{2}+(5\text{i})(-5\text{i}) \\  & ={x}^{2}+25.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we find the quotient when $f(x)$ is divided by ${x}^{2}+25$ using polynomial division.

$$
\begin{aligned} & \,\,\,\,\,\,x-1\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\, \\  & {x}^{2}+25\,\,\enclose{longdiv}{\,\,{x}^{3}-{x}^{2}+25x-25\,} \\  & \,\,\,\,\,\,{{x}^{3}+25x}_{―} \\  & \,\,\,\,\,\,\,-{x}^{2}\,-25 \\  & \,\,{\,-{x}^{2}\,\,-25}_{―} \\  & \,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,0\end{aligned}
$$

  

Thus, $f(x)=({x}^{2}+25)(x-1).$ 

To find the remaining root, we set the linear factor equal to zero and solve for $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}x-1=0\,⟹\,x=1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the roots are $x=1$ and $x=\pm \,5\text{i}.$

canonical_examples.problem: Given that $x=-2$ is a solution to the equation $x^3+8 = 0,$ find the remaining solutions.
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Let $f(x) = x^3+8.$ Since $x=-2$ is a root of $f(x),$ then according to the factor theorem $(x+2)$ is a factor of $f(x).$ 

We find the quotient when $f(x)$ is divided by $(x+2)$ using synthetic division.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14065202/assets/a92f1e322fc91c8388e7969117aca8e616625128d82ee12c88ce108cb6b2637e.png)

Thus, $f(x) = (x+2)(x^2-2x+4).$ 

To find the remaining two roots, we solve $x^2-2x+4 = 0$ by completing the square:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}-2x+4 & =0 \\ {x}^{2}-2x+1+3 & =0 \\ (x-1)^{2}+3 & =0 \\ (x-1)^{2} & =-3 \\ (x-1)^{2} & ={(\sqrt{3}\text{i})}^{2} \\ x-1 & =\pm \sqrt{3}\text{i} \\ x & =1\pm \sqrt{3}\text{i}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solutions to our original equation are $x=-2, \, 1\pm \sqrt3\textrm{i}.$

canonical_examples.problem: Find all of the solutions to $x^3-3x^2+12x-10 = 0$ given that $x=1+3\text{i}$ is a solution.
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
First, we let $f(x) = x^3-3x^2+12x-10.$ 

Since $f(x)$ has real coefficients and $x_1=1+3\text{i}$ is a root of $f(x),$ the complex conjugate 

$$
\overline{x_1}=\overline{1+3\textrm{i}}=1-3\text{i}
$$

must also be a root of $f(x).$

Now, according to the factor theorem, 
$\big(x-(1+3\text{i})\big)\big(x-(1-3\text{i})\big)$
is a factor of $f(x).$ Expanding the parentheses, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}(x-(1+3\text{i}))(x-(1-3\text{i})) & = \\ {x}^{2}-(1+3\text{i}+1-3\text{i})x+(1+3\text{i})(1-3\text{i}) & = \\ {x}^{2}-2x+({1}^{2}-(3\text{i})^{2}) & = \\ {x}^{2}-2x+10 & .\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we find the quotient when $f(x)$ is divided by $x^2 - 2x + 10$ using polynomial division.

$$
\begin{aligned} & \,\,\,\,\,\,x-1 \\  & {x}^{2}-2x+10\,\,\enclose{longdiv}{\,\,{x}^{3}-3{x}^{2}+12x-10\,\,} \\  & \,\,\,\,\,\,{{x}^{3}-2{x}^{2}+10x}_{―} \\  & \,\,\,\,\,\,-{x}^{2}+2x-10 \\  & \,\,\,\,\,\,{\,-\,{x}^{2}+2x-10}_{―} \\  & \,\,\,\,\,\,0\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, $f(x) = (x^2 - 2x + 10)(x-1).$ 

To find the remaining root, we set the linear factor equal to zero and solve for $x\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}x-1=0\,⟹\,x=1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the roots are $x=1, 1 \pm 3\textrm{i}.$
